For an in-depth explanation of how {C.HYPERTABLE}s and {C.HYPERCORE} work, see the [Data model](/learn/deep-dive/whitepaper#data-model).

This page shows you how to get the best results when you set a policy to automatically convert {C.CHUNK}s in a {C.HYPERTABLE}
from the {C.ROWSTORE} to the {C.COLUMNSTORE}.

The code samples in this page use the [crypto_sample.zip](https://assets.timescale.com/docs/downloads/candlestick/crypto_sample.zip) data from [this key features tutorial](/get-started/quickstart/quickstart-5-minutes).

## Optimize your data with {C.COLUMNSTORE} policies

The compression ratio and query performance of data in the {C.COLUMNSTORE} is dependent on the order and structure of your
data. Rows that change over a dimension should be close to each other. With time-series data, you `orderby` the time
dimension. For example, `Timestamp`:

| Timestamp  | Device ID  |  Device Type |  CPU |Disk IO|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|12:00:01|A|SSD|70.11|13.4|

This ensures that records are compressed and accessed in the same order. However, you would always have to
access the data using the time dimension, then filter all the rows using other criteria. To make your queries more
efficient, you segment your data based on the following:

- The way you want to access it. For example, to rapidly access data about a
single device, you `segmentby` the `Device ID` column. This enables you to run much faster analytical queries on
data in the {C.COLUMNSTORE}.
- The compression rate you want to achieve. The [lower the cardinality](https://www.tigerdata.com/blog/what-is-high-cardinality) of the `segmentby` column, the better compression results you get.

When {C.TIMESCALE_DB} converts a {C.CHUNK} to the {C.COLUMNSTORE}, it automatically creates a different schema for your
data. It also creates and uses custom indexes to incorporate the `segmentby` and `orderby` parameters when
you write to and read from the {C.COLUMNSTORE}.

## Migrate an existing {C.HYPERTABLE} to {C.HYPERCORE}

If you already have a {C.HYPERTABLE} with data in the {C.ROWSTORE}, you have two paths to convert existing {C.CHUNK}s to the {C.COLUMNSTORE}. Both start with the same step: enable the {C.COLUMNSTORE} and set `segmentby` and `orderby` on the {C.HYPERTABLE}.

```sql
ALTER TABLE metrics SET (
  timescaledb.enable_columnstore,
  timescaledb.segmentby = 'device_id',
  timescaledb.orderby = 'time DESC'
);
```

These settings apply to {C.CHUNK}s that have not yet been converted to the {C.COLUMNSTORE}. For an existing {C.HYPERTABLE} that has never used {C.HYPERCORE}, that means every {C.CHUNK}.

### Hands-off: add a {C.COLUMNSTORE} policy

Add a [columnstore policy](/reference/timescaledb/hypercore/add_columnstore_policy). The policy runs as a background {C.JOB} and converts eligible {C.CHUNK}s on its own schedule:

```sql
CALL add_columnstore_policy('metrics', after => INTERVAL '7d');
```

This is the recommended path for most workloads. The {C.JOB} runs single-threaded, so for a large backlog the initial conversion can take a while to catch up.

### Manual: convert {C.CHUNK}s yourself

For finer control — for example, to convert a large backlog faster — call [convert_to_columnstore](/reference/timescaledb/hypercore/convert_to_columnstore) on individual {C.CHUNK}s. List the {C.CHUNK}s first:

```sql
SELECT show_chunks('metrics', older_than => INTERVAL '7d');
```

Then convert them. {C.CHUNK}s are converted independently, so you can run `convert_to_columnstore` on distinct {C.CHUNK}s from multiple sessions in parallel:

```sql
-- Session 1
CALL convert_to_columnstore('_timescaledb_internal._hyper_1_2_chunk');

-- Session 2 (concurrent)
CALL convert_to_columnstore('_timescaledb_internal._hyper_1_3_chunk');
```

Each call takes an exclusive lock on the {C.CHUNK} it is converting. Different {C.CHUNK}s do not block each other, so parallel sessions speed up an initial migration. Match the degree of parallelism to your service's available CPU and I/O.

<Callout variant="warning">

Conversion contends on locks with any concurrent write to the same {C.CHUNK}. If you are backfilling old data while a {C.COLUMNSTORE} policy or a manual `convert_to_columnstore` call is running, the two operations wait on each other and one can fail or stall. For a clean migration, pause the {C.COLUMNSTORE} policy while backfilling. Find the `job_id` first:

```sql
SELECT job_id FROM timescaledb_information.jobs
WHERE proc_name = 'policy_compression' AND hypertable_name = 'metrics';
```

Then pause it:

```sql
SELECT alter_job(<JOB_ID>, scheduled => false);
```

Finish the backfill, convert the affected {C.CHUNK}s, then re-enable the policy with `alter_job(<JOB_ID>, scheduled => true)`. For the full pause-backfill-reconvert workflow, see [convert_to_rowstore](/reference/timescaledb/hypercore/convert_to_rowstore).

</Callout>

## Reference

For integers, timestamps, and other integer-like types, data is compressed using [delta encoding](/learn/columnar-storage/compression-methods#delta-encoding),
[delta-of-delta](/learn/columnar-storage/compression-methods#delta-of-delta-encoding), [simple-8b](/learn/columnar-storage/compression-methods#simple-8b), and [run-length encoding](/learn/columnar-storage/compression-methods#run-length-encoding). For columns with few
repeated values, [XOR-based](/learn/columnar-storage/compression-methods#xor-based-compression) and [dictionary compression](/learn/columnar-storage/compression-methods#dictionary-compression) is used. For all other types,
[dictionary compression](/learn/columnar-storage/compression-methods#dictionary-compression) is used.
